Chapter 1 listed the 8 domain names; this deck opens each one in turn. The number badge (1–8) on each domain’s title slide keeps the order: stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty. For each domain learn its purpose, its key terms (many are examined as definitions), and one or two practices you could describe in a scenario answer. Project Performance Domains SE423: Software Project Management 1 d
Project Performance Domains

Definition : a project performance domain is a group of related activities that are critical for the effective delivery of project outcomes. The domains are interactive, interrelated and interdependent areas of focus that work in unison: weak stakeholder engagement hurts planning, poor measurement hides uncertainty, and so on. They run concurrently throughout the project, whether value is delivered frequently, periodically or only at the end. They are not phases done in order, which is exactly the trap in the real MCQ. Which of the following best explains the nature of project performance domains? 5111 all The we coverdcostus principles Project Performance Domains The GuidedBehaviors whichare ProjectPerformancdeomain The • A project performance domain is a group of related activities that are critical for the effective delivery of project outcomes. • Project performance domains are interactive, interrelated, and interdependent areas of focus that work in unison to achieve desired God project outcomes. go 095 • Performance domains run concurrently throughout the project, regardless of how value is delivered (frequently, periodically, or at the end of the project). 2
Slide 3

Stakeholder : an individual, group or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity or outcome of a project, program or portfolio. All three count: someone who only believes they are affected is still a stakeholder. Stakeholder analysis : systematically gathering and analysing quantitative and qualitative information to decide whose interests to take into account throughout the project. It covers stakeholders internal and external to the organization, and those who support, oppose or are neutral toward the project. Ignoring opponents is how projects get blocked late. Edugate scheduling system: identify three main stakeholder groups for this project, describe their roles, and explain how their input will shape the system. 1 Stakeholder Performance Domain https://vt.tiktok.com/ZSHsX4HEr/ • Stakeholder • An individual, group, or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity, or outcome of a project, program, or portfolio. • Stakeholder Analysis told • A method of systematically gathering and analyzing quantitative and qualitative information to determine whose interests should be taken into account throughout the project. • includes stakeholders who are internal and external to the organization, those who are supportive of the project, and those who may not be supportive or are neutral. 3
Stakeholder Performance Domain

Technical PM skills matter, but interpersonal and leadership skills for working with stakeholders may matter more. Most stakeholder problems (resistance, conflicting expectations) are solved by listening, negotiating and building trust, not by a better Gantt chart. The circles diagram groups stakeholders from the core team outward to customers, end users and regulators. Stakeholder Performance Domain • Technical project management skills are important, but having the interpersonal and leadership skills to work effectively with stakeholders is maybe more important. 4
Checking Outcomes: Stakeholder Performance Domain

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Here: a productive working relationship with stakeholders throughout, checked by observing it and by how stakeholders move along the engagement continuum (unaware → resistant → neutral → supportive → leading). Stakeholder agreement with project objectives , checked by the number of changes: many scope modifications suggest stakeholders weren’t aligned. Supportive beneficiaries and harmless opponents , checked with surveys, interviews and focus groups, and by reviewing the issue and risk registers. Checking Outcomes of Stakeholder Performance Domain 5
Team Performance Domain

The team domain covers the activities and functions of the people who produce the project deliverables. Desired outcomes: shared ownership of the work, a high-performing team , and leadership and interpersonal skills shown by all team members, not only the PM. 2 Team Performance Domain StakeholdersTeams 6
Project Team Management and Leadership

Project management applies knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to both management and leadership activities. Management focuses on the means of meeting objectives: effective processes, planning, coordinating, measuring and monitoring work. It manages things. Leadership focuses on people : influencing, motivating, listening, enabling. It leads people. Both are needed to deliver the outcomes. Influencing, motivating and listening to the team are examples of which kind of activity? Project Team Management and Leadership • Project management entails applying knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques for management activities as well as leadership activities. • Management activities focus on the means of meeting project objectives, such as having effective processes, planning, coordinating, measuring, and monitoring work, among others. • Leadership activities focus on people. • Leadership includes influencing, motivating, listening, enabling, and other activities having to do with the project team. • Both are important in delivering the intended outcomes. 7
Project Team Management and Leadership

Leadership should be practised by everyone , but management activities can be centralized or distributed. In a centralized environment, accountability (being answerable for an outcome) is usually assigned to one person, the PM or a similar role. A project charter or other authorizing document gives that PM approval to form the team and use resources. Project Team Management and Leadership • Centralized Management and Leadership • While leadership activities should be practiced by all project team members, management activities may be centralized or distributed. • In an environment where management activities are centralized, accountability (being answerable for an outcome), is usually assigned to one individual, such as the project manager or similar role. • In these situations, a project charter (see example in notes below) or other authorizing document can provide approval for the project manager to form a project team to achieve the project outcomes. 8
Project Team Management and Leadership

In distributed management, PM activities are shared among a project management team while team members do the work. A team may even self-organize to complete the project. Instead of a designated PM, someone acts as facilitator to enable communication, collaboration and engagement (like a Scrum master), and the role can shift among members. Project Team Management and Leadership • Distributed Management and Leadership • Sometimes project management activities are shared among a project management team, and project team members are responsible for completing the work. • There are also situations where a project team may self-organize to complete a project. • Rather than having a designated project manager, someone within the project team may serve as facilitator to enable communication, collaboration, and engagement. • This role may shift among project team members. 9
Centralized vs. Decentralized

Decentralized : middle and lower-level managers have decision power, and authority goes to those closer to the stakeholders ; units are self-sufficient. Centralized : a few upper-management members decide, with authority at the top of the chain of command. Decentralized gives faster decisions and more creativity but is more expensive (duplicated resources and skills in each unit). Centralized gives more standardization and control and is less expensive , with limited creativity. Learn it as three opposite pairs: speed vs. control, more vs. less expensive, creativity vs. standardization. In decentralized project management, decision-making authority is primarily: Which is a characteristic of decentralized management, according to the table? Project Team Management and Leadership AW 10
Project Team Management and Leadership

Whatever the structure, most teams need the same foundations: a shared vision and objectives , clear roles and responsibilities , and agreed team operations (how meetings, decisions and communication work). Guidance : for the whole team, to keep everyone heading the same way, and from individual members on particular tasks or deliverables. Growth : point out what the team does well and where it can improve, then set improvement goals together (what a retrospective does). Sentence, in slide order: V ery R ich P eople G et G old. Vision and objectives, Roles and responsibilities, Project team operations, Guidance, Growth. Project Team Management and Leadership • Common Aspects of Team Development • Regardless of how the management activities are structured, there are common aspects of project team development that are relevant for most project teams. • These include: • Vision and objectives. • Roles and responsibilities. • Project team operations. • Guidance. • Guidance can be directed to the overall project team to keep everyone headed in the right direction. • Individual project team members may also provide guidance on a particular task or deliverable. • Growth. • Identifying areas where the project team is performing well and pointing out areas where the project team can improve helps the project team to grow. • Working collaboratively, the project team can identify goals for its improvement and take steps to meet those goals. 11
Project Team Culture

Every team develops its own culture . It can be built deliberately , by agreeing team norms (“we review every pull request within a day”), or form informally from how members actually behave. It operates within the organization’s culture but reflects the team’s own ways of working. Project Team Culture • Each project team develops its own team culture. • The project team’s culture may be established deliberately by developing project team norms, or informally through the behaviors and actions of its project team members. • The project team culture operates within the organization’s culture but reflects the project team’s individual ways of working and interacting. 12
Project Team Culture

The PM is key to a safe, respectful, nonjudgmental environment where people can speak openly (the basis of trust in Chapter 3). The main way is modeling the behaviors the PM wants: transparency, integrity, respect, positive discourse, support and courage (raising problems, admitting mistakes). Celebrating success is one of them: recognizing milestones and contributions keeps morale high. CRyPTICS : Courage, Respect, Positive discourse, Transparency, Integrity, Celebrating success, Support. Your team has just completed a major milestone in the project development process. How would you celebrate this achievement collaboratively with your team members? How would you recognize individual contributions to the team’s success? What actions would you take to ensure that team morale remains high as you move forward in the project? Project Team Culture • The project manager is key in establishing and maintaining a safe, respectful, nonjudgmental environment that allows the project team to communicate openly. • One way to accomplish this is by modeling desired behaviors, such as: • Transparency • Integrity • Respect • Positive discourse • Support • Courage • Celebrating success 13
High-Performing Project Teams

Factors of high-performing teams. Open communication, shared understanding of goals and shared ownership of the work: everyone knows what they are building and feels it is theirs. Trust and collaboration : members rely on each other and work together instead of protecting their own part. Adaptability and resilience : the team adjusts to change and recovers from setbacks. Empowerment (the team can make decisions) and recognition (contributions are acknowledged). R oller COASTERS : Recognition, then Collaboration, Open communication, Adaptability, Shared understanding, Trust, Empowerment, Resilience, Shared ownership. What are key characteristics of a good team? High-Performing Project Teams • The list below identifies some of the factors associated with high- performing project teams. • Open communication • Shared understanding • Shared ownership • Trust • Collaboration • Adaptability • Resilience • Empowerment • Recognition 14
Leadership Skills

Vision : establish and maintain a shared picture of what the project is for, so decisions point the same way. Critical thinking : weigh evidence, question assumptions and make sound judgments. Motivation : understand what drives each person (intrinsic or extrinsic) and use it. Interpersonal skills : emotional intelligence, decision-making and conflict resolution (next slide). MICE : Motivation, Interpersonal skills, Critical thinking, Establishing and maintaining vision. Leadership Skills Establishing and Maintaining Vision Critical Thinking Motivation Interpersonal Skills 15
Components of Emotional Intelligence

Emotional intelligence (EI) has four components: two about yourself, two about others. Self-awareness : how do you affect the team, and how does the team affect you? Self-management : think before you act, build trust. Social awareness : be empathetic, use active listening. Social skill : establish rapport, build effective teams, manage attitude. “Be empathetic” and “employ active listening” belong to which component of emotional intelligence? Components of Emotional Intelligence 16
Tailoring Leadership Styles

Leadership styles (autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire, transactional, servant…) are tailored to the project, environment and stakeholders; no style is always right. What drives the choice: experience with this type of project, the maturity of the team members (a senior team needs less direction), the organization’s governance structure , and whether the team is distributed (which needs more deliberate communication). DEMO : Distributed teams, Experience with the project type, Maturity of team members, Organizational governance. How can a project manager balance technical leadership with adaptive leadership in a software team? Tailoring Leadership Styles • leadership styles (ex: autocratic, democratic, laisser-faire, transactional, servant, etc.) are tailored to meet the needs of the project, the environment, and the stakeholders. • Some of the variables that influence tailoring of leadership styles include: • Experience with the type of project • Maturity of the project team members • Organizational governance structures • Distributed project teams 17
Checking Outcomes: Team Performance Domain

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Team: shared ownership (members are engaged and take initiative), a high-performing team (trust, collaboration, adapting to change) and leadership shown by all (evidenced by members’ interpersonal skills and initiative). Checking Outcomes—Team Performance Domain 18
Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain

This domain covers the development approach , cadence and life-cycle phases . Outcomes: approaches that are consistent with the deliverables , and a life cycle whose phases connect the delivery of value from start to end and support the required delivery cadence . 3 Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain 19
Development Approach and Life Cycle

Deliverable : any unique and verifiable product, result or capability that must be produced to complete a process, phase or project. Development approach : the method used to create and evolve the product: predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive or hybrid. Cadence : a rhythm of activities conducted throughout the project (two-week sprints, monthly releases). A predictable rhythm helps coordination and communication. Project phase : a set of logically related activities ending in one or more deliverables. Project life cycle : the series of phases from start to completion. In project management, what is the primary purpose of establishing a project cadence? Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain: • Deliverable • Any unique and verifiable product, result, or capability to perform a service that is required to be produced to complete a process, phase, or project. • Development Approach. • A method used to create and evolve the product, service, or result during the project life cycle, such as a predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive, or hybrid method. • Cadence. • A rhythm of activities conducted throughout the project. • Project Phase. • A collection of logically related project activities that culminates in the completion of one or more deliverables. • Project Life Cycle. • The series of phases that a project passes through from its start to its completion. 20
Development, Cadence, and Life Cycle

The chain of decisions starts with the type of deliverable : it determines how the product can be developed (you can’t release half a bridge, but you can release half an app). The deliverable type and approach then influence the number and cadence of deliveries … …and the approach plus the desired cadence determine the life cycle and its phases . Delivery cadence is the timing and frequency of deliveries. Projects can have a single delivery (at the end), multiple deliveries (at different points), or periodic deliveries (on a fixed schedule, e.g. monthly). Development, Cadence, and Life Cycle • The type of project deliverable(s) determines how it can be developed. • The type of deliverable(s) and the development approach influence the number and cadence for project deliveries. • The deliverable approach and the desired delivery cadence determine the project life cycle and its phases. • Delivery cadence refers to the timing and frequency of project deliverables. • Projects can have a single delivery, multiple deliveries, or periodic deliveries. 21
Delivery Cadence

For digital products there is a fourth option: continuous delivery . It delivers feature increments immediately to customers, using small batches of work and automation (automated build, test and deployment). From the product perspective the emphasis is delivering value throughout the product’s life, so the team can respond to market trends. It is part of DevOps , #noprojects and Continuous Digital (Chapter 4 covers DevOps). Delivery Cadence • For digital products, another delivery option is called continuous delivery. • Continuous delivery is the practice of delivering feature increments immediately to customers, often through the use of small batches of work and automation technology. • From the product management perspective, the emphasis is on delivering benefits and value throughout the product life cycle. • This allows the team to respond to market trends and stay focused on value delivery. • This practice is included in several approaches such as DevOps, #noprojects and Continuous Digital, for example. 22
Development Approaches

A development approach is the means used to create and evolve the product during the life cycle. Industries use different names for the same approaches. The three common ones are predictive, hybrid and adaptive , a spectrum rather than three boxes: the further toward adaptive, the more iterative and incremental the work. HeAP : Hybrid, Adaptive, Predictive. Development Approaches • A development approach is the means used to create and evolve the product, service, or result during the project life cycle. • There are different development approaches, and different industries may use different terms to refer to development approaches. • Three commonly used approaches are • predictive, • hybrid, and • adaptive. 23
Development Approaches

Predictive (waterfall) is useful when requirements can be defined, collected and analysed at the start . It is also used when there is significant investment and high risk that call for frequent reviews, change control and replanning between phases (a new hospital information system). Scope, schedule, cost, resources and risks can be defined early and are relatively stable . It reduces uncertainty early and does most of the planning up front . A government payroll system must implement fixed legal rules that will not change during the project. Which development approach fits, and why? Development Approaches • Predictive approach • A predictive approach is useful when the project and product requirements can be defined, collected, and analyzed at the start of the project. (Waterfall approach) • May also be used when there is a significant investment involved and a high level of risk that may require frequent reviews, change control mechanisms, and replanning between development phases. • The scope, schedule, cost, resource needs, and risks can be well defined in the early phases of the project life cycle, and they are relatively stable. • This development approach allows the project team to reduce the level of uncertainty early in the project and do much of the planning upfront. 24
Development Approaches

Hybrid combines elements of adaptive and predictive approaches. It is useful when there is uncertainty or risk around the requirements for part of the product. It also fits when deliverables can be modularized or built by different teams: a fixed back-end integration planned predictively, with a user-facing app built in sprints. Edugate scheduling system: given the evolving requirements (student usability, advisor requests, IT integration rules), which development approach (Agile, Waterfall, or Hybrid) would you recommend, and why would it be the best fit for this project? Development Approaches • Hybrid approach • A hybrid development approach is a combination of adaptive and predictive approaches. • This means that some elements from a predictive approach are used and some from an adaptive approach are used. • This development approach is useful when there is uncertainty or risk around the requirements. • Hybrid is also useful when deliverables can be modularized, or when there are deliverables that can be developed by different project teams. 25
Iterative vs. Incremental

Iterative (top row): try different ideas to clarify scope, approach and requirements, refining the same thing after each round of feedback (sketch → mock-up → prototype → app). The customer needs a way to capture ideas that might change. Incremental (bottom row): progressively add new features and functions, each a working piece (foundation → frame → walls → finished house), with feedback after each increment. Adaptive approaches use both. Iterative refines; incremental adds. Adding one new working feature to the product in each cycle is best described as: Development Approaches • Hybrid approach 26
Development Approaches

Adaptive approaches suit requirements with high uncertainty and volatility that will change throughout the project. A clear vision is set at the start; the known requirements are then refined, detailed, changed or replaced based on user feedback, the environment or unexpected events. Adaptive approaches are iterative and incremental ; toward the far adaptive end, iterations get shorter and the product evolves more from stakeholder feedback. In which type of project would an iterative development approach be most beneficial? Development Approaches • Adaptive approach • Adaptive approaches are useful when requirements are subject to a high level of uncertainty and volatility and are likely to change throughout the project. • A clear vision is established at the start of the project, and the initial known requirements are refined, detailed, changed, or replaced in accordance with user feedback, the environment, or unexpected events. • Adaptive approaches use iterative and incremental approaches. However, on the far side of the adaptive methods, the iterations tend to get shorter and the product is more likely to evolve based on stakeholder feedback. 27
Development Approaches

Agility is a mindset broader than any framework, but agile approaches count as adaptive. Some use 1–2 week iterations that end with a demonstration of what was accomplished. The team is very engaged in planning each iteration. It decides how much scope it can achieve from a prioritized backlog , estimates the work itself, and works collaboratively through the iteration to build it. Development Approaches • Adaptive approach • While agility is a wide mindset that is broader than a development framework, agile approaches can be considered adaptive. Some agile approaches entail iterations that are 1 to 2 weeks in duration with a demonstration of the accomplishments at the end of each iteration. • The project team is very engaged with the planning for each iteration. • The project team will determine the scope they can achieve based on a prioritized backlog, estimate the work involved, and work collaboratively throughout the iteration to develop the scope. 28
Considerations for Selecting Approaches

Product variables that influence the approach. Rule of thumb: high innovation , uncertain requirements , unstable scope , easy change and frequent delivery options push toward adaptive. Strict safety requirements and regulations push toward predictive (they need documented, controlled phases). Sentence, in slide order: D on’t R ush S cope: E very D elivery R isks S afety R ules. Degree of innovation, Requirements certainty, Scope stability, Ease of change, Delivery options, Risk, Safety requirements, Regulations. A medical device must meet strict safety regulations and its requirements are stable. Which way do these product variables push the development approach? Considerations for Selecting Approaches • There are many variables associated with the nature of the product or service that influence the development approach. • Degree of innovation • Requirements certainty • Scope stability • Ease of change • Delivery options • Risk • Safety requirements • Regulations 29
Considerations for Selecting Approaches

Project variables: stakeholders, schedule constraints and funding availability . Stakeholders : adaptive methods need significant stakeholder involvement throughout; a product owner sets and prioritizes the work. Schedule : if something must be delivered early , even unfinished, an iterative or adaptive approach helps. Funding : under funding uncertainty , adaptive or iterative work is safer… …because a minimum viable product (MVP) can be released with less investment to test or capture the market. SaFeS : Stakeholders, Funding availability, Schedule constraints. Considerations for Selecting Approaches • Project variables that influence the development approach are centered around stakeholders, schedule constraints, and funding availability. • Stakeholders • Projects that use adaptive methods require significant stakeholder involvement throughout the process. • Certain stakeholders, such as the product owner, play a substantial role in establishing and prioritizing work. • Schedule constraints • If there is a need to deliver something early, even if it is not a finished product, an iterative or adaptive approach is beneficial. • Funding availability • Projects that work in an environment of funding uncertainty can benefit from an adaptive or iterative approach. • A minimum viable product can be released with less investment than an elaborate product. • This allows for market testing or market capture with minimum investment. 30
Considerations for Selecting Approaches

Organizational variables also matter: structure, culture, capability, team size and location . A strongly hierarchical, documentation-heavy culture struggles with adaptive work; a small co-located team adopts it easily; large or distributed teams need more structure. SuCCeSs : Structure, Culture, Capability, Size and location of the team. Considerations for Selecting Approaches • The Organization • Organizational variables such as the structure, culture, capability, project team size, and location influence the development approach. • Organizational structure • Culture • Organizational capability • Project team size and location 31
Life Cycle and Phase Definition

Phases often end with a phase gate review (stage gate): a checkpoint that the phase’s desired outcomes or exit criteria are met before moving on. Exit criteria may be tied to acceptance criteria for deliverables, contractual obligations or performance targets. The diagrams: a predictive life cycle (feasibility → design → build → test → deploy → close, one phase after another) and an incremental one (plan → design → build repeated, each round delivering an increment). Life Cycle and Phase Definition • Project phases often have a phase gate review (also known as stage gate) to check that the desired outcomes or exit criteria for the phase have been achieved before proceeding to the next phase. mme • Exit criteria may tie to acceptance criteria for deliverables, contractual obligations, meeting specific performance targets, or other tangible measures. Sample Incremental Development Approach Sample Predictive Life Cycle 32
A hybrid life cycle: the community center

A real hybrid example. The community center building follows predictive phases with milestone reviews: start up → plan → development → test → deploy → close. Inside development, the website is delivered in iterations (senior service releases 1–4) and the training (community action patrol modules 1–3 and integration) in increments, while construction proceeds predictively. One project, different approaches for different deliverables. 33
Checking Outcomes: Development Approach and Life Cycle

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Development approach and life cycle: approaches consistent with the deliverables (an approach that suits each product), a life cycle that delivers value from start to end , and phases that support the delivery cadence . Checking Outcomes—Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain 34
Planning Performance Domain

The planning domain covers the initial, ongoing and evolving organization and coordination needed to deliver the deliverables and outcomes. Desired outcomes: the project progresses in an organized, coordinated way; a holistic approach to delivery; evolving information elaborated over time; planning time appropriate for the situation (not over-planning); enough information to manage stakeholder expectations; and a process to adapt plans as needs change. 4 Planning Performance Domain 35
Planning Performance Domain

Estimate : a quantitative assessment of the likely amount or outcome of a variable (cost, resources, effort, duration). Accuracy = correctness : how well the estimate predicts reality. Estimate $100K, actual $102K → accurate. Precision = exactness : how detailed and consistent the estimate is. A precise estimate (every cost broken down) can still be inaccurate if the project ends up costing much more. Accurate = hits the target; precise = tightly grouped. An estimate built from a detailed, line-by-line cost breakdown ends up 40% over the actual cost. The estimate was: Planning Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Planning Performance Domain: • Estimate • A quantitative assessment of the likely amount or outcome of a variable, such as project costs, resources, effort, or durations. • Accuracy correctness • Within the quality management system, accuracy is an assessment of correctness: Reflects how well your plan predicts reality (If you estimate a project will cost $100K and it ends up costing $102K, your estimate was accurate) • Precision exact • Within the quality management system, precision is an assessment of exactness: Reflects the level of detail and consistency in your planning assumptions (if your estimates are based on a precise breakdown of the costs): An estimate can be precise because all the details are taken into account but not accurate if the project ends up costing much more or much less. 36
Planning Overview

The purpose of planning is to proactively develop an approach to create the deliverables: deciding in advance instead of reacting. High-level planning may start before the project is authorized (to build the business case). The team progressively elaborates early documents (vision statement, charter, business case): start high-level, add detail as more is learned. Planning increasingly weighs social and environmental impacts as well as financial ones, e.g. a product life cycle assessment of materials, toxicity and sustainability. Planning Overview • The purpose of planning is to proactively (ʦ̷̎ ɑ ˀˣ) develop an approach to Ą ɒ create the project deliverables. • High-level planning may begin prior to project authorization. • The project team progressively elaborates initial project documents, such as a vision statement, project charter, business case, or similar documents to identify or define a coordinated path to achieve the desired outcomes. • It is becoming more common for initial planning to consider social and environmental impacts in addition to the financial. Such as a product life cycle assessment which evaluates the potential environmental impacts of a product, process, or system (impacts of materials and processes with regards to sustainability, toxicity, and the environment). 37
Planning

Planning starts by understanding the business case , the stakeholder requirements, and the project and product scope. Product scope : the features and functions of the product, service or result (what it has). Project scope : the work performed to deliver it (what the team must do). Don’t swap them; near-identical terms are the instructor’s favourite trap. Describe the significance of a project scope statement in project management and elaborate on how it aids in mitigating project risks and ensuring successful project outcomes. “The work performed to deliver a product, service, or result with the specified features and functions” defines: Planning • Planning begins with understanding the business case, stakeholder requirements, and the project and product scope. • Product scope defines the features and functions that characterize a product, service, or result. • Project scope also defines the work performed to deliver a product, service, or result with the specified features and functions. 38
Delivery

Predictive planning starts with high-level deliverables and decomposes them using a scope statement and a work breakdown structure (WBS) . Iterative and incremental planning decomposes themes or epics into features, then into user stories and other backlog items. Work that is unique, significant, risky or novel is done first, to reduce scope uncertainty before big investment. Routine work is planned at the last responsible moment : defer a decision to keep options open until the cost of further delay would exceed the benefit. Deferring a decision until the cost of further delay would exceed the benefit of waiting is called: Delivery • In predictive planning approaches • start with the high-level project deliverables upfront and decompose them into more detail. • Employ a scope statement and/or a work breakdown structure (WBS) to decompose the scope into lower levels of detail. • In Iterative and Incremental planning • can have high-level themes or epics that are decomposed into features, which are then further decomposed into user stories and other backlog items. • Work that is unique, significant, risky, or novel can be prioritized to reduce the uncertainty associated with project scope at the start of the project before significant investment has taken place. • Project teams plan routine work based on the concept of last responsible moment. • This approach defers a decision to allow the project team to consider multiple options until the cost of further delay would exceed the benefit. 39
Estimating

Planning develops estimates for effort, duration, costs, people and physical resources . An estimate is a quantitative assessment of a likely amount or outcome. Estimates change as the project evolves and more is known (the “cone of uncertainty” in Chapter 6). To plan accurately for the design, prototyping, and testing phases, you need to estimate the time and effort required. Choose two effort estimation techniques you would apply to this project. Explain how each technique supports better planning and risk control in this scenario. Estimating • Planning entails developing estimates for work effort, duration, costs, people, and physical resources. • Estimates are a quantitative assessment of the likely amount or outcome of a variable, such as project costs, resources, effort, or duration. • As the project evolves, the estimates can change based on current information and circumstances. 40
Schedules

A schedule is a model for executing the activities: durations, dependencies and other planning information. It can be planned predictively or adaptively . The predictive steps: (1) decompose scope into activities; (2) sequence them; (3) estimate effort, duration and resources; (4) allocate people and resources by availability; (5) adjust until the schedule is agreed. Decompose → sequence → estimate → allocate → adjust. The order matters here: D ogs S neak E very A pple A way. Decompose, Sequence, Estimate, Allocate, Adjust. As the project manager, you must ensure that the 12-month development timeline is realistic and achievable. Identify three project scheduling methods/techniques you would use to plan the sequence and timing of tasks. Briefly explain how each method helps in identifying delays or managing overlapping activities. Schedules • A schedule is a model for executing the project’s activities, including durations, dependencies, and other planning information. • Schedule planning can use predictive or adaptive approaches. • Predictive approaches follow a stepwise process as follows: • Step 1. Decompose the project scope into specific activities. • Step 2. Sequence related activities. • Step 3. Estimate the effort, duration, people, and physical resources required to complete the activities. • Step 4. Allocate people and resources to the activities based on availability. • Step 5. Adjust the sequence, estimates, and resources until an agreed-upon schedule is achieved. 41
Schedules

Mandatory : required by contract or by the nature of the work (you can’t test code before it is written). Usually cannot be modified. Discretionary : based on best practice or preference (“finish the design review before coding”). May be modified, which is what fast-tracking relaxes. External : between a project activity and a non-project one (waiting for a government permit or a vendor’s delivery). Usually cannot be modified. Internal : between project activities, under the team’s control. May be modified. DIME : Discretionary, Internal, Mandatory, External. Waiting for a government permit before construction can begin is which type of dependency? Schedules • The four types of dependencies are: • Mandatory dependency • A relationship that is contractually required or inherent in the nature of the work. This type of dependency usually cannot be modified. • Discretionary dependency • A relationship that is based on best practices or project preferences. This type of dependency may be modifiable. • External dependency • A relationship between project activities and non-project activities. This type of dependency usually cannot be modified. • Internal dependency • A relationship between one or more project activities. This type of dependency may be modifiable. 42
Schedules

Adaptive scheduling uses incremental planning . A high-level release plan says which features go in each release. Each release contains two or more iterations … …and each iteration adds business or stakeholder value (features, risk reduction, experiments). Future releases are kept high level on purpose, because feedback from earlier releases will change them. Schedules • Adaptive schedule planning uses incremental planning. • One such scheduling approach is based on iterations and releases. • A high-level release plan is developed that indicates the basic features and functionality to be included in each release. • Within each release, there will be two or more iterations. • Each iteration adds business and/or stakeholder value. • Value may include features, risk reduction, experimentation, or other ways of delivering or protecting value. • The planning for the work in future releases is kept at a high level so the project team does not engage in planning that could change based on feedback from earlier releases. 43

Adaptive approaches use timeboxes : fixed time, flexible scope (a sprint). The work in each timebox comes from a prioritized backlog . The team decides how much it can do, estimates it, and self-manages to complete it. At the end the team demonstrates the completed work… …and the backlog and estimates are updated and reprioritized for the next timebox. Schedules • Adaptive approaches often use timeboxes. • The work in each timebox is based on a prioritized backlog. • The project team determines the amount of work they can do in each timebox, estimates the work, and self-manages to accomplish the work. • At the end of the timebox, the project team demonstrates the work completed. • At that point, the backlog and estimates of work available to be done may be updated or reprioritized for the next timebox. 45
Budget

The budget grows out of the agreed estimates. Cost estimates are aggregated into the cost baseline … …which is a time-phased budget : spread across the schedule to show when costs will be incurred. That lets the PM balance the funds approved per budget period against the scheduled work. If a period’s funding is limited, work may have to be rescheduled to fit. Budget • The project budget evolves from the agreed estimates for the project. • Cost estimates are then aggregated to develop the cost baseline. • The cost baseline (time-phased budget) is often allocated across the project schedule to reflect when the costs will be incurred. • This practice allows project managers to balance the funds approved in a specific budget period with the scheduled work. • If there are funding limitations for a budget period, the work may need to be rescheduled to meet those limitations. 46
Budget

The budget should include contingency reserve for uncertainty. Contingency reserve : set aside to implement a risk response or respond to identified risks if they occur. Controlled by the PM . (“Known unknowns”.) Management reserve : set aside for unknown , unexpected in-scope work. Usually controlled by upper management . (“Unknown unknowns”.) Depending on the organization, management reserve may be held by the project, the sponsor, the product owner or the PMO . A reserve for unknown, unplanned in-scope work, usually controlled by upper management, is the: Budget • The project budget should include contingency reserve funds to allow for uncertainty. • Contingency reserves are set aside to implement a risk response or to respond to risk events should they occur (for identified risks, controlled by PM). • Management reserves are set aside for unexpected activities related to in-scope work (for unknown risks, usually controlled by upper management). • Depending on the organization’s policies and organizational structure, management reserves may be managed by the project, the sponsor, product owner, or the PMO at the program and portfolio level. 47
Budget Build Up

Build the budget bottom-up: work cost estimates come first. Add the contingency reserve → the cost baseline (what the PM manages against). Add the management reserve → the total project budget . So contingency is inside the baseline; management reserve is outside it. Which amount is included in the cost baseline but not in the management reserve? Budget Build Up 48

Physical Resources • Physical resources apply to any resource that is not a person. • It can include materials, equipment, software, testing environments, licenses, and so forth. • Planning for physical resources entails estimating, as well as supply chain, logistics, and management. • Projects with significant physical resources, such as engineering and construction projects, will need to plan for procurement activities to acquire the resources. • Planning for physical resources includes taking into account lead time for delivery, movement, storage, and disposition of materials, as well as a means to track material inventory from arrival on site to delivery of an integrated product. 49

Deciding which deliverables to develop in-house and which to purchase is called: Procurement • Procurement can happen at any time during a project. However, upfront planning helps to set expectations that ensure the procurement process is performed smoothly. • Once the high-level scope is known, project teams conduct a make-or- buy analysis. • This includes identifying those deliverables and services that will be developed in-house, and those that will be purchased from external sources. • This information impacts the project team and the schedule. 50
Metrics

Planning, delivering and measuring work are naturally linked… …and the link is metrics . Decide what to measure and how often by the rule “only measure what matters” : measuring costs effort. Metrics • There is a natural linkage between planning, delivering, and measuring work. • That linkage is metrics. • Establishing metrics includes setting the thresholds that indicate whether work performance is as expected, trending positively or negatively away from expected performance, or unacceptable. • Deciding what to measure and “how often” is best informed by the phrase “only measure what matters.” 51

Leading a project means understanding its constraints . They include fixed delivery dates , regulatory compliance, a predetermined budget and quality policies. Constraints shift during the project. Checking Outcomes: Measurement

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Measurement: a reliable understanding of status (audits of measures), actionable data (data shows whether to act), timely action (leading indicators prevent surprises) and business value from informed decisions. Checking Outcomes—Measurement Performance Domain 87
Uncertainty Performance Domain

The uncertainty domain covers activities related to risk and uncertainty. Outcomes: awareness of the environment (technical, social, political, market, economic), proactive exploration of and response to uncertainty, awareness of how variables depend on each other, anticipating threats and opportunities, delivery with little impact from surprises, and opportunities realized. And cost and schedule reserves used effectively to stay aligned with the objectives. 8 Uncertainty Performance Domain 88
Uncertainty Performance Domain

Uncertainty : a lack of understanding or awareness of issues, events, paths or solutions. Ambiguity : being unclear, having difficulty identifying the cause of events, or having multiple options to choose from. Complexity : a characteristic that makes a project difficult to manage because of human behavior, system behavior and ambiguity. Volatility : the possibility of rapid and unpredictable change . Risk : an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on objectives. CRAVe : Complexity, Risk, Ambiguity, Volatility. “The possibility for rapid and unpredictable change” defines: Uncertainty Performance Domain • The following definitions are relevant to the Uncertainty Performance Domain: • Uncertainty • A lack of understanding and awareness of issues, events, paths to follow, or solutions to pursue. • Ambiguity • A state of being unclear, having difficulty in identifying the cause of events, or having multiple options from which to choose. • Complexity • A characteristic of a program or project or its environment that is difficult to manage due to human behavior, system behavior, and ambiguity. • Volatility • The possibility for rapid and unpredictable change. • Risk • An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives. 89
Uncertainty Performance Domain

Uncertainty in the broadest sense is a state of not knowing or unpredictability. It has nuances: risk (not knowing future events), ambiguity (not being aware of current or future conditions) and complexity (dynamic systems with unpredictable outcomes). Uncertainty Performance Domain • Uncertainty in the broadest sense is a state of not knowing or unpredictability. • There are many nuances to uncertainty, such as: • Risk associated with not knowing future events, • Ambiguity associated with not being aware of current or future conditions, and • Complexity associated with dynamic systems having unpredictable outcomes. 90
Uncertainty Performance Domain

Navigating uncertainty starts with understanding the larger environment . Sources: economic (price volatility, resource availability, borrowing, inflation), technical (new technology, system complexity, interfaces), legal , physical (safety, weather, working conditions), ambiguity, and social and market influences shaped by opinion and media. Political influences, inside or outside the organization. (A PESTLE-style checklist.) PLATE SPinning : Political, Legal, Ambiguity, Technical, Economic, Social and market, Physical. Uncertainty Performance Domain • Successfully navigating uncertainty begins with understanding the larger environment within which the project is operating. • Aspects of the environment that contribute to project uncertainty include, but are not limited to: • Economic factors such as volatility in prices, availability of resources, ability to borrow funds, and inflation/deflation; • Technical considerations such as new or emerging technology, complexity associated with systems, and interfaces; • Legal or legislative constraints or requirements; • Physical environment as it pertains to safety, weather, and working conditions; • Ambiguity associated with current or future conditions; • Social and market influences shaped by opinion and media; and, • Political influences, either external or internal to the organization. 91
Ambiguity

Conceptual ambiguity : a lack of shared understanding, when people use the same terms differently. “The schedule was reported on track last week”: was it on track last week, or was it reported last week? Disagreeing about what “done” means is the same problem. Situational ambiguity : more than one outcome is possible; having several options to solve a problem is a form of it. Team members argue in a status meeting because they mean different things by “done”. Which kind of uncertainty is this? Ambiguity • There are two categories of ambiguity: • Conceptual ambiguity • The lack of effective understanding—occurs when people use similar terms or arguments in different ways. • For example, the statement, “The schedule was reported on track last week,” is not clear. • It isn’t clear whether the schedule was on track last week or whether it was reported on last week. • Situational ambiguity • Surfaces when more than one outcome is possible. • Having multiple options to solve a problem is a form of situational ambiguity. 92
Complexity

Complexity makes a project or its environment difficult to manage because of human behavior, system behavior or ambiguity. It exists when there are many interconnected influences that behave and interact in diverse ways. Complexity • Complexity is a characteristic of a program, project, or its environment, which is difficult to manage due to human behavior, system behavior, or ambiguity. • Complexity exists when there are many interconnected influences that behave and interact in diverse ways. 93
Complexity

In complex environments, individual elements combine into unforeseen or unintended outcomes . The effect: there is no way to predict the likelihood of outcomes accurately, or even which outcomes might emerge. Three families of ways to work with complexity: systems-based , reframing and process-based (next three slides). Complexity • In complex environments, it is not uncommon to see an aggregation of individual elements leading to unforeseen or unintended outcomes. • The effect of complexity is that there is no way of making accurate predictions about the likelihood of any potential outcome or even of knowing what outcomes might emerge. • There are numerous ways to work with complexity; some of them are systems-based, some entail reframing, and others are based on process. 94
Systems-Based Complexity

Decoupling (systems-based): disconnect parts of the system to simplify it and reduce connected variables. Understanding how one piece works on its own shrinks the problem. Simulation : use similar but unrelated scenarios to model parts of the system. A new airport with shops and restaurants can study shopping malls to learn about consumer buying habits. A team designing a new airport’s retail area studies shopping malls to predict consumer buying habits. Which complexity technique is this? Systems-Based Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that is systems based include: • Decoupling • Disconnecting parts of the system to both simplify the system and reduce the number of connected variables. • Determining how a piece of a system works on its own reduces the overall size of the problem. • Simulation • There may be similar though unrelated scenarios that can be used to simulate components of a system. • A project to build a new airport that includes an area with shopping and restaurants can learn about consumer buying habits by seeking out analogous information on shopping malls and entertainment establishments. 95
Reframing Complexity

Diversity (reframing): view the system from diverse perspectives, e.g. brainstorming to open divergent ideas, then Delphi-like processes to converge. Balance : balance the type of data used (forecasts and lagging indicators, not just one) for a broader view, and use elements whose variations counteract each other’s negative effects. Reframing Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that entail reframing are: • Diversity • Complex systems require viewing the system from diverse perspectives. • This can include brainstorming with the project team to open up divergent ways of seeing the system. • It can also include Delphi-like processes to move from divergent to convergent thinking. • Balance • Balancing the type of data used rather than only using forecasting data or data that report on the past or lagging indicators provides a broader perspective. • This can include using elements whose variations are likely to counteract each other's potential negative effects. 96
Process-Based Complexity

Iterate (process-based): build iteratively or incrementally, one feature at a time, and after each iteration learn what worked, what didn’t and how customers reacted. Engage : build in stakeholder engagement, which reduces assumptions and builds learning into the process. Fail safe : for critical elements, build in redundancy or graceful degradation so a component failure doesn’t take the whole system down (a backup server). lIFE : Iterate, Fail safe, Engage. Adding a backup server so a critical system keeps working in reduced form if its main server fails is which complexity technique? Process-Based Complexity • Examples of working with complexity that is process based include: • Iterate • Build iteratively or incrementally. • Add features one at a time. After each iteration, identify what worked, what did not work, customer reaction, and what the project team learned. • Engage • Build in opportunities to get stakeholder engagement. • This reduces the number of assumptions and builds learning and engagement into the process. • Fail safe • For elements of a system that are critical, build in redundancy or elements that can provide a graceful degradation of functionality in the event of a critical component failure. 97
Volatility

Volatility exists where change is rapid and unpredictable . It often comes from fluctuations in available skills or materials (a key specialist leaves; chip prices spike). It usually hits cost and schedule . Volatility • Volatility exists in an environment that is subject to rapid and unpredictable change. • Volatility can occur when there are ongoing fluctuations in available skill sets or materials. • Volatility usually impacts cost and schedule. 98
Volatility

Volatility is addressed with alternatives analysis and reserves . Alternatives analysis : find and evaluate different ways to meet the objective: a different mix of skills , resequencing work, or outsourcing . Reserve : a cost reserve covers budget overruns caused by price volatility (and a schedule reserve covers time). Volatility • Alternatives analysis and use of cost or schedule reserve address volatility. • Alternatives analysis • Finding and evaluating alternatives, such as looking at different ways to meet an objective, such as using a different mix of skills, resequencing work, or outsourcing work • Reserve • Cost reserve can be used to cover budget overruns due to price volatility. 99
Risk

Risk is one aspect of uncertainty. It is an uncertain event or condition with a positive or negative effect on objectives if it occurs. Negative risks are threats ; positive risks are opportunities . Every project has risk because projects are unique undertakings. Risk • Risks are an aspect of uncertainty. • A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives. • Negative risks are called threats, and positive risks are called opportunities. • All projects have risks since they are unique undertakings with varying degrees of uncertainty. 100
Risk

Overall project risk is often a function of complexity, ambiguity and volatility . Responses to overall risk use the same strategies as individual threats and opportunities, applied to the project as a whole . If overall risk is too high, the organization may cancel the project: a legitimate outcome, not a failure of risk management. Risk • Overall risk is often a function of complexity, ambiguity, and volatility. Responses to overall project risk are the same as for individual threats and opportunities, though responses are applied to the overall project rather than to a specific event. • If the overall risk on the project is too high, the organization may choose to cancel the project. 101
Risk (Threat)

A threat is an event or condition with a negative impact on objectives if it occurs. Avoid : eliminate the threat or protect the project from it (change the plan, drop the risky feature). Escalate : the threat is outside the PM’s authority or scope, so pass it to the right level (program, portfolio, sponsor). Transfer : shift ownership and impact to a third party (insurance, a fixed-price contract). Mitigate : reduce the probability or impact (extra testing, a prototype). Accept : acknowledge it without action, perhaps with a contingency reserve. Threats, the A TEAM : Accept, Transfer, Escalate, Avoid, Mitigate. Buying insurance against a data-centre fire is which threat response strategy? Risk (Threat) • A threat is an event or condition that, if it occurs, has a negative impact on one or more objectives. • Five alternative strategies may be considered for dealing with threats, as follows: • Avoid • Escalate • Transfer • Mitigate • Accept 102
Risk Reduction over Time

The table scores five risks each month (impact × probability = severity), and the threat profile chart stacks their severities over time. The total (dashed line) falls from about 26 in January to about 11 in April. Some risks disappear as they are dealt with ( permits obtained drops to 0 once permits are secured; “site not ready in time” too), while “pump capacity” stays. A falling profile is the evidence that risk responses are working. Risk Reduction over Time 103
Risk (Opportunities)

An opportunity is an event or condition with a positive impact on objectives if it occurs. Example: a time-and-materials subcontractor finishes early , saving cost and schedule. Exploit : act to make sure the opportunity happens (raise its probability to 100%). Share : give part of the ownership to a third party better able to capture the benefit (a partnership). Enhance : increase its probability or impact without guaranteeing it. Escalate and accept apply to opportunities too. Opportunities, in slide order: E ach E xtra S hare E arns A gain. Exploit, Escalate, Share, Enhance, Accept. A team identifies a chance to finish early and takes action to ensure that the opportunity occurs. Which strategy is this? A firm partners with another company so that both can capture a positive risk neither could capture alone. Which opportunity strategy is this? Risk (Opportunities) • An opportunity is an event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive impact on one or more project objectives. • An example of an opportunity could be a time and materials-based subcontractor who finishes work early, resulting in lower costs and schedule savings. • Five alternative strategies may be considered for dealing with opportunities, as follows: • Exploit • Escalate • Share • Enhance • Accept 104
Risk (Management and Contingency

A reserve is time or budget set aside for handling risks. Contingency reserve : for identified risks, should they occur. Management reserve : for unknown events such as unplanned, in-scope work (slide 47). True or false: contingency reserve is set aside for unknown, unplanned events. Risk (Management and Contingency Reserve) • Reserve is an amount of time or budget set aside to account for handling risks. • Contingency reserve is set aside to address identified risks should they occur. • Management reserve is a budget category used for unknown events such as unplanned, in-scope work. 105
Risk (Risk Review)

A regular cadence of review and feedback with a broad set of stakeholders helps navigate risk proactively. Daily stand-ups (usable in any project) surface potential threats and opportunities. Reported blockers may become threats if they keep delaying progress… …while progress and breakthroughs may point to opportunities to exploit and share. Frequent demonstrations of increments, interim designs or proofs of concept also surface threats and opportunities early. Risk (Risk Review) • Establishing a frequent rhythm or cadence of review and feedback sessions from a broad selection of stakeholders is helpful for navigating project risk and being proactive with risk responses. • Daily standup meetings can be used in any project and are a source for identifying potential threats and opportunities. • Reports of blockers or impediments could become threats if they continue to delay progress. • Likewise, reports of progress and breakthroughs might point toward opportunities to be further leveraged and shared. • Frequent demonstrations of increments of the product or service, interim designs, or proof of concepts can surface threats and opportunities. 106
Checking Outcomes: Uncertainty

The “checking outcomes” table: the left column is what success looks like for the domain, the right column is the evidence that it happened. You won’t be asked to reproduce it, but it is a good structure for a written answer about the domain. Uncertainty: awareness of the environment (environmental factors considered in estimates and plans), proactive responses (risk register and responses kept current), awareness of interdependencies, anticipation of threats and opportunities, little impact from surprises, realized opportunities, and effective use of reserves. 107
