n: Slide 1

Tailoring means fitting the project-management approach to the project. Models, methods and artifacts are the toolbox it picks from. This finishes Chapter 1: principles (how to behave) and performance domains (what to manage) are applied through a tailored selection of tools. Tailoring, Models, Methods, and Artifacts SE423: Software Project Management 1
Outline
Part 1, slides 3–22: tailoring. Part 2, slides 23–41: models, methods and artifacts. Outline • Tailoring • Models, Methods, and Artifacts 2
Tailoring (section)
Section divider: tailoring. Tailoring 3
Tailoring

Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the project-management approach, governance and processes to suit the environment and the work at hand. Deliberate is the key word: it is a conscious design choice, not cutting corners. It covers the development approach , processes, project life cycle, deliverables and who to engage. Many variables drive it, including the project’s criticality and the number of stakeholders. Example: a nuclear reactor needs far more rigor, checks and balances and reporting than a new office building. More critical means more process, never less. Which statement best defines tailoring? Tailoring • Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the project management approach, governance, and processes to make them more suitable for the given environment and the work at hand. • In a project environment, tailoring considers the development approach, processes, project life cycle, deliverables, and choice of people with whom to engage. • Many variables factor into the tailoring process, including the criticality of the project and the number of stakeholders involved. • Using these variables as an example, it is evident that the rigor, checks and balances, and reporting required for a critical project (e.g., building a nuclear reactor) are much greater than those for building a new office building. 4
Tailoring

Tailoring starts with understanding the project’s context, goals and operating environment . Projects must balance competing demands : speed, low cost, value, quality, regulatory compliance, diverse stakeholder expectations, and adapting to change. No project can maximize all seven at once (the fastest delivery is rarely the cheapest or the most thoroughly checked), which is why the approach has to be tailored to what matters most here. COMPADreS : Creating high-quality deliverables, Optimizing value, Minimizing costs, Providing compliance, Adapting to change, Delivering quickly, Satisfying stakeholders. Tailoring • Tailoring involves understanding the project context, goals, and operating environment. • Projects operate in complex environments that need to balance potentially competing demands that include, but are not limited to: • Delivering as quickly as possible, • Minimizing project costs, • Optimizing the value delivered, • Creating high-quality deliverables and outcomes, • Providing compliance with regulatory standards, • Satisfying diverse stakeholder expectations, and • Adapting to change. 5
Why Tailor?

Tailoring brings direct and indirect benefits : More commitment from team members, because they helped shape the approach they now follow. A customer-oriented focus , because the customer’s needs drive the tailoring. More efficient use of resources : effort goes where the project needs it, not into unneeded process. Which is a stated benefit of tailoring? Why Tailor? • Tailoring produces direct and indirect benefits to organizations. • These include, but are not limited to: • More commitment from project team members who helped to tailor the approach, • Customer-oriented focus, as the needs of the customer are an important influencing factor in its development, and • More efficient use of project resources. 6
What to Tailor?

Five aspects can be tailored (slides 8–12 take one each). Life cycle and development approach . Processes . Engagement of people. Tools . Methods and artifacts . TEMPLe : Tools, Engagement, Methods and artifacts, Processes, Life cycle and development approach. What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Life cycle and development approach selection, • Processes, • Engagement, • Tools, and • Methods and artifacts. 7
What to Tailor?

Choosing the life cycle and its phases is a form of tailoring. So is choosing the development and delivery approach . Example: a new data center uses a predictive approach for the building’s construction and finishing, and an iterative approach to discover and establish the computing capabilities it needs. At the project level that combination is hybrid , even though each team only experiences its own approach (the construction team sees predictive, the computing team sees iterative). A new data center is built in fixed construction phases, while its computing capabilities are worked out in iterations. What is the overall approach? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Life cycle and development approach selection, • Deciding on a life cycle and the phases of the life cycle is an example of tailoring. • Additional tailoring can be done when selecting the development and delivery approach for the project. • For instance, building a new data center could involve • (a) the use of predictive approaches for the physical building construction and finishing and • (b) an iterative approach for understanding and establishing the computing capabilities required. • Viewed from a project level, this combination of approaches represents a hybrid approach, but the construction team and the computing team may only experience a predictive or iterative development approach. 8
What to Tailor?

Process tailoring decides which parts of the chosen approach’s processes are: Added (extra rigor, e.g. a security review), modified (changed to fit, e.g. a lighter weekly report), removed (dropped as unnecessary), blended (elements from different methods combined into one, e.g. Scrum ceremonies with a predictive budget process) or aligned (harmonized so definitions and terms are consistent across teams). A RuMBA : Aligned, Removed, Modified, Blended, Added. Combining elements of two different methods into one process is which process-tailoring action? What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Processes, • Process tailoring for the selected life cycle and development approach includes determining which portions or elements should be: • Added • Modified • Removed • Blended • Aligned 9
What to Tailor?

Engagement tailoring decides how people are involved: People : who is on the team and with which skills and capabilities. Empowerment : how much responsibility and local decision-making the team gets (a mature team gets more). Integration : how contractors, partners and other organizations are brought into the team. PIE : People, Integration, Empowerment. What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Engagement, • Tailoring engagement for the people involved in the project includes: • People • Empowerment • Integration 10
What to Tailor?

Choosing the tools (software, equipment) is tailoring. The team usually has the best insight into which tools suit the work, but choices may be tempered by their cost . Organizational leaders may also impose constraints the team can’t change (a mandated corporate tool). What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Tools • Selecting the tools (e.g., software or equipment) the project team will use for the project is a form of tailoring. • Often, the project team has the best insight into the most suitable tools for the situation, but those choices might need tempering based on the associated costs. • Additionally, organizational leaders can impose constraints that the project team cannot change. 11
What to Tailor?

Methods (the means of achieving outcomes) are tailored to fit the environment and culture . Artifacts (documents, templates) are tailored so they are appropriate for the project and organization: a two-page charter for a small internal project, a full one for a regulated contract. What to Tailor? • Project aspects that can be tailored include: • Methods and artifacts • Tailoring the means that will be used to achieve the project outcomes is performed so that the methods are suited for the environment and the culture. • Tailoring the documents, templates, and other artifacts that will be used on the project helps to make sure the artifacts are appropriate for the project and the organization. 12
The Tailoring Process

The tailoring process, step 1 : select the initial development approach : choose the approach best suited to the endeavor (the ticked set of gears). Step 2 : tailor for the organization : modify it to fit organizational requirements and constraints. Step 3 : tailor for the project : adjust for size, criticality and other project factors. Step 4 : implement ongoing improvement : inspect and adapt; the loop arrow shows it never ends. Put the four steps of the tailoring process in order. The Tailoring Process 13
Selecting the Initial Development

Step 1 in pictures: choose the base approach, e.g. agile or waterfall (the handwritten note). Step 2: one set of gears becomes the organization’s adapted version. Step 3: elements are removed (the crossed boxes) and adjusted for this project. Step 4: the remaining process keeps being refined. Selecting the Initial Development Approach Selecting the Initial Development Approach Tailoring the Approach for the Organization waterfall exagile Tailoring the Approach for the Project Implement Ongoing Improvement 14
Assessing the Organizational and Project

Tailoring happens at two levels . At the organizational level, a general PM methodology and development approach are adapted into the organization’s own methodologies, e.g. one for small projects and one for large or sensitive projects. At the project level, each project tailors further (methodologies for projects A–E differ). Both levels are guided by environmental factors , general guides, and the available models, methods and artifacts. Assessing the Organizational and Project Factors When Tailoring 15
Tailoring for the Project

Tailoring for the project depends on many attributes, grouped into three: Product/deliverable (slide 17), project team (slide 18) and culture (slide 19). CoPPer : Culture, Project team, Product or deliverable. Tailoring for the Project • Many attributes influence tailoring for the project. • These include, but are not limited to: • Product/deliverable, • Project team, and • Culture. 16
Tailoring for the Project

Product/deliverable attributes. Compliance and criticality : how much rigor and assurance are needed. Also the type of product, the industry market, the technology and the time frame. Stability of requirements (stable favours predictive, volatile favours adaptive) and security needs. Sentence, in slide order: C ats T ake I n T oo T iny S nacks, S adly. Compliance, Type of product, Industry market, Technology, Time frame, Stability of requirements, Security. Tailoring for the Project • Product/Deliverable • Attributes associated with the product or deliverable include, but are not limited to: • Compliance/criticality • Type of product/deliverable • Industry market • Technology • Time frame • Stability of requirements • Security. 17
Tailoring for the Project

Project team considerations. Team size and geography (co-located or distributed), and how it is distributed across the organization. Team experience (an experienced team needs less prescribed process) and access to the customer (adaptive approaches need frequent customer input). SAGE O wl: Size of the team, Access to customer, Geography, Experience, Organizational distribution. Tailoring for the Project • Project Team • Project team considerations include: • Project team size • Project team geography • Organizational distribution • Project team experience • Access to customer 18
Tailoring for the Project

Culture is the organization’s shared norms, beliefs and practices . Tailoring checks how the approach fits it: is the culture formal and hierarchical, agile and collaborative , risk-averse or innovation-driven? An agile process forced onto a strictly hierarchical culture struggles. Evaluate buy-in (support from key stakeholders), trust , empowerment and the organizational culture as a whole. TO BE : Trust, Organizational culture, Buy-in, Empowerment. Tailoring for the Project • Culture (refers to the shared norms, beliefs, and practices within a company.) • When tailoring a project, you assess how the project management approach fits with this culture—whether it's formal and hierarchical, agile and collaborative, risk-averse, or innovation-driven. • Evaluating the culture includes considerations regarding: • Buy-in (gaining support and commitment from key stakeholders, especially those who influence or are affected by the project) • Trust • Empowerment • Organizational culture 19
Implement Ongoing Improvement

Tailoring is not a one-time exercise done at the start. During progressive elaboration , problems with how the team works or how the product evolves show where more tailoring would help. Review points, phase gates and retrospectives are the opportunities to inspect and adapt the process, the approach and the delivery frequency. True or false: tailoring is done once, when the project is initiated. Implement Ongoing Improvement • The process of tailoring is not a single, one-time exercise. • During progressive elaboration, issues with how the project team is working, how the product or deliverable is evolving, and other learnings will indicate where further tailoring could bring improvements. • Review points, phase gates, and retrospectives all provide opportunities to inspect and adapt the process, development approach, and delivery frequency as necessary. 20
Situations and Tailoring Suggestions

The pattern in this table: name the problem, then tailor in the missing control. Poor quality deliverables → add feedback, verification loops and quality-assurance steps. Members unsure how to proceed → add guidance, training and verification. Long approval delays → streamline decisions: fewer people authorized to decide, up to value thresholds. Too much work in progress or scrap → value-stream mapping and kanban boards to visualize the work and find the problems. Disengaged stakeholders → check information sharing and feedback loops; deeper engagement may work better than simply communicating. Lack of visibility of progress → make sure the right measures are collected, analysed and discussed, and validated with the team and stakeholders. Recurring surprises → root-cause analysis of gaps in the process. A team keeps waiting several days for approvals before it can proceed. What tailoring change does the table suggest? 21
Summary

Summary: tailoring is the considered adaptation of approach, governance and processes to the environment and project. It involves analysing, designing and deliberately modifying the people, processes and tools . Four steps: select the initial approach → tailor for the organization → tailor for the project → implement ongoing improvement . The order matters here: S mart T eams T ailor I teratively. Select the initial approach, Tailor for the organization, Tailor for the project, Implement ongoing improvement. Summary • Tailoring involves the considered adaptation of approach, governance, and processes to make them more suitable for the given environment and the project at hand. • It involves the analysis, design, and deliberate modification of the people elements, the processes employed, and the tools used. • The tailoring process involves four steps: • Select initial approach • Tailor for the organization • Tailor for the project • Implement ongoing improvement 22
Models, Methods, and Artifacts (section)
Section divider: models, methods and artifacts. Models, Methods, and Artifacts 23
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

This section gives a high-level description of common models, methods and artifacts. It is not exhaustive or prescriptive : a menu of options to tailor from, not a checklist to use every time. Models, Methods, and Artifacts • This section provides a high-level description of some commonly used models, methods, and artifacts that are useful in managing projects. • The items listed in this section are not intended to be exhaustive or prescriptive, but rather to help project teams think about the options available to them. 24
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

A model is a thinking strategy that explains a process, framework or phenomenon (e.g. Tuckman explains how teams develop). A method is the means for achieving an outcome, output, result or deliverable (e.g. estimating, a retrospective). An artifact is a template, document, output or deliverable (e.g. a risk register, a project charter). Model = think, method = do, artifact = thing. MaMA : Model, Method, Artifact. A risk register is best classified as a: Give an example of a project management tool or technique that you might use to manage a complex software development project, and explain how it could help you ensure project success. Models, Methods, and Artifacts • Model • A model is a thinking strategy to explain a process, framework, or phenomenon. • Method • A method is the means for achieving an outcome, output, result, or project deliverable. • Artifact • An artifact can be a template, document, output, or project deliverable. detitarable is a Goodexamk project 25
Principles, domains and the toolbox together

The whole PMBOK 7 picture in one diagram. At the top, the 12 principles … … guide behavior in… …the 8 performance domains (the circle), which are carried out with models, methods and artifacts (left and right) to produce deliverables. Everything sits inside the system for value delivery and the internal and external environments, and is tailored to fit the project context (bottom). 26
Models, Methods, and Artifacts

Every model, method and artifact has costs : time, the expertise needed to use it, the impact on productivity. Teams should weigh these before adopting one. Avoid anything that duplicates work or adds unnecessary effort, isn’t useful to the team and stakeholders, produces incorrect or misleading information, or serves one individual’s needs rather than the team’s (a report one manager likes but nobody reads). Models, Methods, and Artifacts • As with any process, the use of models, methods, and artifacts has associated costs related to time, level of expertise/proficiency in use, impact on productivity, etc. • Project teams should consider these implications when deciding which elements to use. • As much as possible, project teams should avoid using anything that: • Duplicates or adds unnecessary effort, • Is not useful to the project team and its stakeholders, • Produces incorrect or misleading information, or • Caters to individual needs versus those of the project team. 27
Commonly Used Models

Situational Leadership II : the PM adapts style to each member’s development level (competence and commitment): directing a beginner, coaching, supporting, then delegating to an expert. The instructor’s note: understand these models, don’t memorize them. OSCAR (Outcome, Situation, Choices/consequences, Actions, Review): a coaching model for guiding conversations, solving problems and developing people. Communication models : cross-cultural communication (principles for communicating across cultures) and the effectiveness of communication channels (clarity, speed, richness, recordability, accessibility, suitability): pick the channel that fits the message. Gulf of execution and evaluation (from UX): the gap between a user’s goal and what the system lets them do, and between the system’s response and the user’s ability to interpret it. This chapter (from Pinto’s Project Management ) looks at the three organizational features that shape how projects are run: strategy (why projects exist), structure (who reports to whom and how resources are shared) and culture (the unwritten rules people follow). Projects and Organizational Strategy

Strategic management is the science of formulating, implementing and evaluating cross-functional decisions that enable an organization to achieve its objectives. Cross-functional matters: strategy cuts across departments, and so do the projects that carry it out. It starts by developing vision and mission statements , then formulates, implements and evaluates strategies, making cross-functional decisions along the way… …all aimed at achieving the organization’s objectives . What is the main purpose of strategic management? Projects and Organizational Strategy Strategic management: the science of formulating, implementing, and evaluating cross-functional decisions that enable an organization to achieve its objectives. Consists of: • Developing vision and mission statements • Formulating, implementing, and evaluating • Making cross-functional decisions • Achieving objectives Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. The table’s point: projects are how strategy gets implemented . Each strategic intention on the left becomes a type of project on the right. A strategy of greater market penetration becomes new product development projects; a strategy of more efficient business processes becomes reengineering projects; operating initiatives become new or modernized plants. Matching competitors’ products becomes reverse engineering ; better cross-organization communication in the supply chain becomes enterprise IT efforts; better departmental coordination becomes concurrent engineering. Strategy example: the Airbus A380

The Airbus A380 case: what went wrong was mainly strategic , not execution. Airbus and Boeing saw the same facts (air traffic doubling every 15 years). Airbus concluded the future needed much bigger planes to serve congested hub airports, and built the A380. Boeing concluded that medium-sized wide-body jets flying directly between more cities fitted the future better, and the market followed Boeing. Lesson: a project can be well run and still fail if the strategy behind it is wrong. What went wrong for the A380? Much of the blame rests on the strategic decisions taken by Airbus and its view of the future of global aviation. At the beginning of the millennium, Airbus and Boeing looked where their business was heading and saw similar facts: air traffic doubling every 15 years, including estimates that the number of travelers would hit four billion by 2020—and came to radically different conclusions for the future. For Airbus there was need for much bigger planes for sustainable growth at congested airports. For Boeing, medium-sized wide-body jets best matched future globalization pressures and anticipated higher frequency of travel among major and multiple growing cities. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Projects and Organizational Strategy

Vision and mission statements state what the organization hopes to accomplish or become. Formulating, implementing and evaluating : projects are the key ingredients in strategy implementation . The firm evaluates opportunities by setting its vision, assessing internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats, setting long-range objectives, and choosing among alternatives. Cross-functional decisions and achieving objectives complete the process. The TOWS matrix turns SWOT into strategies: SO (use strengths to seize opportunities), ST (use strengths against threats), WO (overcome weaknesses using opportunities), WT (minimize weaknesses and avoid threats). The order matters here: D on’t F orget M y A im. Developing vision and mission, Formulating strategy, Making cross-functional decisions, Achieving objectives. In a TOWS matrix, a strategy that uses internal strengths to take advantage of external opportunities is called: Projects and Organizational Strategy Strategic management consists of the following elements 1. Developing vision statements and mission statements. Vision and mission statements establish a sense of what the organization hopes to accomplish or what top managers hope it will become at some point in the future. 2. Formulating, implementing, and evaluating. Projects, as the key ingredients in strategy implementation, play a crucial role in the basic process model of strategic management. A firm devotes significant time and resources to evaluating its business opportunities through developing a corporate vision or mission, assessing internal strengths and weaknesses as well as external opportunities and threats, establishing long-range objectives, and generating and selecting among various strategic alternatives 3. Making cross-functional decisions. 4. Achieving objectives. TOWS Matrix Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Stakeholder Management

Organizations and project teams can’t ignore the external effects of their decisions. Stakeholder analysis shows how the PM and the project relate to the rest of the organization… …and exposes the seemingly irresolvable conflicts that new projects create (a new system that helps sales may burden operations). Project stakeholders : all individuals or groups with an active stake in the project who can affect its development positively or negatively. Stakeholder Management Organizations and project teams cannot operate in ways that ignore the external effects of their decisions. One way to understand the relationship of project managers and their projects to the rest of the organization is through employing stakeholder analysis. Stakeholder analysis is a useful tool for demonstrating some of the seemingly irresolvable conflicts that occur through the planned creation and introduction of new projects. Project stakeholders are defined as all individuals or groups who have an active stake in the project and can potentially impact, either positively or negatively, its development. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Identifying Project Stakeholders

Internal stakeholders : top management, the accountant, other functional managers, project team members. External stakeholders : clients, competitors , suppliers, and environmental, political, consumer and other intervenor groups. Intervenor groups are external groups with the power to intervene and disrupt a project. Environmental groups used lawsuits and lobbying to halt the Dakota Access Pipeline and delay the Keystone XL pipeline for years. Organizational Structure

Organizational structure has three elements. (1) Formal reporting relationships : who reports to whom, how many levels the hierarchy has, and each manager’s span of control (how many people report to them). (2) Groupings : individuals into departments and departments into the organization. (3) Systems that ensure effective communication, coordination and integration of effort across departments. Projects cut across departments, so this third element is where they succeed or struggle. g11 Organizational Structure Consists of three key elements: 1. Designates formal reporting relationships, Who reports to whom? – number of levels in the hierarchy – span of control 2. Identifies groupings of – individuals into departments – departments into the total organization 3. Design of systems to ensure – effective communication – coordination – integration of effort across departments Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Forms of Organization Structure

Functional organizations group people who perform similar activities into departments (marketing, finance, engineering). Project organizations group people into project teams on temporary assignments . Matrix organizations create a dual hierarchy in which functions and projects have equal prominence: staff report to both a functional manager and a project manager. PerFuMe : Project, Functional, Matrix. How are employees grouped in a functional organization? Which statement best describes a project organization? Forms of Organization Structure • Functional organizations—group people performing similar activities into departments • Project organizations—group people into project teams on temporary assignments • Matrix organizations—create a dual hierarchy in which functions and projects have equal prominence Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. Project Organizational Structure

In a project organization each project is a self-contained business unit with a dedicated team . The firm assigns resources from functional pools directly to the project for as long as they are needed . Firms whose business is projects organize this way: construction companies , Boeing and Airbus, pharmaceutical firms, and many software consulting and R&D organizations. Project Organizational Structure Within the project organization, each project is a self- contained business unit with a dedicated project team. The firm assigns resources from functional pools directly to the project for the time period they are needed. Project organizations are those that are set up with their exclusive focus aimed at running projects. Construction companies, large manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus, pharmaceutical firms, and many software consulting and research and development organizations are organized as pure project organizations. Heavyweight Project Organizations

Organizations sometimes benefit from a fully dedicated project organization: a heavyweight project team. Lockheed’s Skunk Works model: a small, autonomous team of hand-picked, highly skilled people with complete freedom, and a PM with full authority, status and responsibility. In heavyweight organizations PM authority is expanded … …functional alignment is abandoned in favour of market opportunism, with direct reporting to the top executives… …and the focus is on the external customer . Project Management Offices

Project management offices (PMOs) are centralized units that oversee or improve the management of projects. They act as resource centres for technical details , expertise , a repository (templates, lessons learned, past project data) and a center of excellence for PM practice. A PMO shifts some of the burden of PM work (activity scheduling, resource allocation, monitoring and control) from the project manager to dedicated support staff. CRaTE : Center for excellence, Repository, Technical details, Expertise. What is a Project Management Office (PMO) and its role in organizations? Project Management Offices Centralized units that oversee or improve the management of projects Resource centers for: • Technical details • Expertise • Repository • Center for excellence Using a PMO as a resource center shifts some of the burden for PM activities (activity scheduling, resource allocation, monitoring, control processes, etc.) from the project manager to a support staff that is dedicated to providing this assistance Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Alternative Levels of Project Offices

A PMO can sit at three levels. Level 3, corporate : serves an overall corporate support function. Level 2, business unit : serves the needs within one business unit or function. Level 1, project : decentralized to the individual project, giving direct support. The numbering runs upward: Level 1 is the narrowest scope, Level 3 the widest. A PMO that serves the needs within one specific business unit is at which level? Alternative Levels of Project Offices The PMO may be situated at a corporate level (Level 3), where it serves an overall corporate support function. It can be placed at a lower functional level (Level 2), where it serves the needs within a specific business unit. Finally, the PMO can be decentralized down to the actual project level (Level 1), where it offers direct support for each project. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Forms of P M O s and Control

Three forms of PMO, by how much control they exert. Supportive (low control): consultative; provides templates, best practices, training and access to information. Controlling (moderate control): requires compliance with adopted PM standards, templates and processes, e.g. through audits. Directive (high control): directly manages the projects; the PMs belong to it. SCoreD , from low control to high: Supportive, Controlling, Directive. A PMO that requires projects to comply with its adopted standards and templates, but does not run the projects itself, is which form? Forms of PMOs and Control Three forms of PMOs, varying with degrees of control and influence include: • Supportive, low control; consultative and provide PM resources and training • Controlling, moderate control; requires compliance to adopted PM standards/processes • Directive, high control; directly manages projects Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Models of P M O s

Three models of PMO, by purpose (not to be confused with the forms, which are about how much control). Weather station : only monitors and tracks project status, without trying to influence or control projects. Control tower : treats PM as a skill to be protected and supported ; it improves methodology and practices and helps PMs apply them. Resource pool : maintains and supplies a cadre of skilled project managers and professionals to the company’s projects. CRoW : Control tower, Resource pool, Weather station. A consultancy keeps a bench of certified project managers and assigns them to client projects as needed. Which PMO model is this? Models of PMOs In addition to the forms of PMO and varying levels of control, there are three models of PMOs with various purposes for companies: • Weather station—the PMO is typically used only as a monitoring and tracking device (management wants to keep an eye on the status of the projects without directly attempting to influence or control them) • Control tower—project management is a skill to be protected and supported (focus on improving methodology and practices and help PM apply them) • Resource pool—maintain and provide a cadre of skilled project professionals (supplying project managers and other skilled professionals to the company’s projects) Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Organizational Culture

The third contextual variable is organizational culture . Definition : the unwritten rules of behavior , or norms, that shape and guide behavior, shared by some subset of organizational members and taught to all new members. The four parts: unwritten (rarely written down); rules of behavior (how to react to events); held by a subset (not necessarily company-wide: engineering can have a different culture from sales); taught to new members (newcomers pick it up by watching others). Example: a culture that rewards collaboration between functional groups. HURT : Held by a subset of the organization, Unwritten, Rules of behavior, Taught to new members. Organizational Culture • The third key contextual variable in how projects are managed effectively is that of organizational culture • Definition of culture: “organization’s culture refers to the unwritten rules of behavior, or norms that are used to shape and guide behavior, that are shared by some subset of organizational members and that are taught to all new members of the company” – Unwritten (are often not written down) – Rules of behavior (guidelines as to how best to react to these events) – Held by some subset of the organization (may or may not be companywide) – Taught to all new members (New members of an organization pick up the behaviors as they observe others engaging in them) • Ex: Company X has a strong supportive culture that emphasizes and rewards positive collaboration between functional groups. Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. All Rights Reserved
Key Factors That Affect Culture

Factors that shape culture: technology , environment (the industry and market), geographical location… … reward systems , rules and procedures, and key organizational members. GE’s jet-engine division and Rolls-Royce make the same product for the same markets, yet GE rewards aggressiveness and high commitment (with high burnout) while Rolls-Royce is paternalistic and rewards loyalty and long tenure, largely because of what each rewards. Critical incidents : moments when the real culture becomes visible, e.g. how leadership reacts to a failed project. CRaG TREK : Critical incidents, Reward systems, Geographical location, Technology, Rules and procedures, Environment, Key organizational members. However, GE prides itself on its competitive, • Geographical location high-pressure culture that rewards aggressiveness and high commitment but also has a high burnout rate among engineers and • Reward systems mid-level managers. Rolls-Royce, on the other hand, represents an example of a much more • Rules and procedures paternalistic culture that rewards loyalty and long job tenure. “ • Key organizational members • Critical incidents (moments when real culture becomes visible) Copyright © 2019, 2016, 2013 Pearson Education, Inc. Organizational Culture: Effects on Project Management

Culture affects project management in four ways. Departmental interaction : cultures where functions actively cooperate with projects succeed far more than disinterested or adversarial ones. Employee commitment to goals : a culture of commitment (extra effort when needed) beats one where going through the motions is fine as long as you don’t get caught. Project planning : where lateness is punished, people pad their estimates to protect themselves; a culture of trust produces honest estimates. Performance evaluation : if the organization quietly rewards caution and playing it safe, its projects will be cautious too. Tuckman's Model for Team Development

Tuckman’s model . Forming : the group comes together and members get to know each other; they are polite and depend on the leader. Storming : a chaotic competing for leadership and trials of group processes; members compete for influence or control, often without clear structure or authority. The PM’s job here is to surface and manage the conflict, not suppress it. Norming : agreement is reached on how the group operates (roles, norms, ways of working). Performing : the group practices its craft and becomes effective at meeting its objectives. Adjourning : the team dissolves at the end of the project. Order: form → storm → norm → perform → adjourn. The order matters, and they rhyme: F orm, S torm, N orm, P erform, then A djourn. According to Tuckman’s model of team development, which stage is characterized by members competing for leadership and struggling with group processes? The stage where the team reaches agreement on how it will operate is: Tuckman's Model for Team Development 1. Forming: The group comes together and gets to initially know one another and form as a group. 2. Storming: A chaotic competing for leadership and trials of group processes (compete for influence or control, often without clear structure or authority) 3. Norming: Eventually agreement is reached on how the group operates 4. Performing: The group practices its craft and becomes effective in meeting its objectives 5. Dissolving/Adjourning 8

Building Trust

Trust is the foundation of teamwork : without it teams struggle to collaborate, share ideas or resolve conflict. Trust is about vulnerability . Vulnerability-based trust means admitting mistakes, asking for help and saying “I don’t know” without fear it will be used against you. This list was a real midterm question. It takes time (consistent behavior, follow-through on commitments, shared experiences under pressure) and must be maintained : one broken promise can undo months. A technique: behavioral profiling (e.g. Myers-Briggs) helps people admit strengths and weaknesses openly; the PM can adjust assignments to match strengths and create a psychologically safe space. What does vulnerability-based trust involve? How does fostering trust and managing conflict within a software project team contribute to improved collaboration and project success? Building Trust • Trust is the foundation of teamwork (Without trust, teams struggle to collaborate, share ideas, or resolve conflict) • Trust is all about vulnerability, which is difficult for most people: Vulnerability- based trust means: Admitting mistakes, Asking for help, Saying “I don’t know” • Takes time (Trust isn’t built overnight. It requires: Consistent behavior, Follow-through on commitments, Shared experiences—especially under pressure) • Needs to be maintained over time. • Techniques – Behavioral profiling (like MyersBriggs). Helps to admit strengths & weaknesses: (Ex: Recognize their introverted tendencies, Adjust task assignments to match their strengths, Create a psychologically safe space for participation) 11
Establishing a basis of trust

Trust is earned, not granted : a title doesn’t make people trust you, and most people are naturally wary of others. This models the vulnerability you want from the team. Lead by example , not by mandate: show the standard you expect. Keep commitments ; if you can’t, give notice and an explanation, not an excuse. Managing Conflict

Healthy conflict is unfiltered, passionate debate around issues , not people, and it requires trust underneath. Even in the best teams it will sometimes be uncomfortable ; that is normal, not a sign of failure. Conflict norms are the team’s rules of engagement (tone, language, timing, emotional expression); they differ per team and must be discussed and made explicit. Avoidance is costly : teams that fear conflict fall into groupthink (harmony over critical thinking), suppress dissent and make poor decisions nobody challenged. Why is healthy conflict important in teams? A team values harmony so much that it stops critically evaluating ideas. This is: Managing Conflict • Good (healthy) conflict among team members requires trust, which is all about engaging in unfiltered, passionate debate around issues. • Even among the best teams, conflict will at times be uncomfortable. • Conflict norms will vary in each team, and must be discussed and made clear: oNorms = rules of engagement: These define what’s acceptable in debate—tone, language, timing, emotional expression. • The fear of occasional personal conflict should not deter a team from having regular, productive debate: oAvoidance is costly: Teams that fear conflict often fall into groupthink (psychological phenomenon where a cohesive group prioritizes harmony and consensus over critical thinking and realistic decision-making), suppress dissent (actively prevent or silence disagreement, criticism, or opposition), or make poor decisions. 14
Managing Conflict – How?

Confronting (problem solving) : resolve the root cause through open, honest dialogue. Gives the most lasting result. Compromising : both sides give something up to reach a middle ground. Quick, but nobody gets what they needed. Withdrawal delays or sidesteps the conflict; smoothing keeps harmony by downplaying differences. Both leave the cause in place. Collaborating : integrate multiple perspectives into a creative solution. With confronting, the preferred approach for a team. Forcing : impose a solution through authority or pressure. Fast in an emergency, but it costs buy-in. The problem-solving steps : define the real/root problem → analyze it → identify solutions → pick one → implement it → review that it solved the problem. How can the project manager encourage collaboration? (Saying “negotiation” alone is not enough: explain.) A PM ends a debate by declaring “we use my design, end of discussion.” Which technique is this? Managing Conflict – How? • Conflict Resolution Techniques • Confronting (Problem Solving): Resolve the root cause through open, honest dialogue • Compromising: Reach a middle ground by mutual concessions • Withdrawal (Avoidance): Delay or sidestep the conflict • Smoothing (Accommodating): Preserve harmony by downplaying differences • Collaborating: Integrate multiple perspectives to find a creative solution • Forcing: Impose a solution through authority or pressure • Problem Solving 1. Define the real/root problem 2. Analyze the problem 3. Identify Solutions 4. Pick a Solution 5. Implement a solution 6. Review the solution, and confirm that it solved the problem 15
ict

Every team meets conflict: successful teams resolve it, unsuccessful ones push it into the background where it festers. Disagreement ≠ conflict . A disagreement is about an idea; a conflict involves a hardening of position and intractability (nobody will move). Almost every conflict traces back to a clash between two parties. Those outside the conflict stay neutral , even if they agree with one side, and one of them acts as conciliator , mediating to defuse the situation. The goal is to reduce the conflict back to a disagreement that can be settled by consensus. Finally, aim for reconciliation between the two parties so the working relationship survives. Disagreement and conflict are the same thing. Managing and resolving conﬂ ict • Every team encounters conﬂict: successful teams resolve conﬂicts, while unsuccessful teams force conﬂict to the background • Disagreement is not the same as conﬂict: conﬂict involves a hardening of position and associated intractability (insolvability) • Virtually all conﬂicts can be traced to a clash between two parties • To preserve a team’s effectiveness, those outside the conﬂict must assume a neutral stance, even if they themselves agree with one of the parties to the conﬂict • One of those outside the conﬂict must take on the role of conciliator; he or she must mediate between the two parties to defuse the situation • The goal is to reduce the conﬂict to a disagreement which can then be addressed through consensus • Strive for reconciliation between the conﬂicting parties, if possible 16
Commitment

Commitment (the third layer) requires clarity and buy-in . Clarity : everyone knows exactly what was decided, why it matters and what is expected next. Teams avoid assumptions and ambiguity and end each discussion with an explicit decision. Buy-in : members support the decision even if they didn’t fully agree, because they trust the process and felt heard (this is why healthy conflict comes first). Buy-in does not require consensus : great teams can disagree and still commit (“disagree and commit”). A common trap: “commitment requires everyone to agree” is false. CuB : Clarity, Buy-in. In the context of the Team Needs Pyramid, explain how a project manager can foster commitment among team members. Team buy-in requires that every member agrees with the decision. Achieving Commitment • Commitment requires clarity & buy-in: • Clarity ensures everyone knows exactly what was decided, why it matters, and what’s expected next. • Buy-in means team members support the decision—even if they didn’t fully agree—because they trust the process and feel heard. • Clarity requires that teams avoid assumptions and ambiguity, and end discussions with a clear understanding about what they’ve decided upon. • Buy-in does not require consensus. Members of great teams learn to disagree with one another and still commit to a decision. 17

Embracing Accountability

On a strong team accountability happens directly among peers : members hold each other to standards instead of waiting for the manager. The leader must show a willingness to confront accountability : be transparent, follow through, and address underperformance respectfully but firmly. If the PM avoids it, so will the team. The best opportunity is during meetings and regular reviews of accomplishments, e.g. at a sprint review: “We committed to five stories but completed three. Let’s explore what happened and how we can improve.” Note the tone: about the commitment, not blaming a person. What’s the best time to reinforce accountability? During a sprint deployment, a key feature was discovered to be not thoroughly tested and caused issues after release. As the project manager, what steps would you follow to address this issue and ensure accountability within the team? Your software project team is experiencing delays due to unclear task ownership and inconsistent updates. As the project manager, how would you apply a team-based approach to improve accountability and transparency within the team? Describe specific steps you would take to enhance collaboration and increase the project’s chances of success. Embracing Accountability • Accountability on a strong team occurs directly among peers: In high- performing teams, members don’t just rely on the manager to enforce standards—they hold each other accountable. • For a culture of accountability to thrive, a leader must demonstrate a willingness to confront accountability: A project manager should model transparency, follow through on commitments, and address underperformance respectfully but firmly. • Best opportunity occurs during meetings and regular review of accomplishments. Example: During a sprint review, the PM might say, “We committed to five stories but completed three. Let’s explore what happened and how we can improve next sprint.” 19

A Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM) is a resource planning tool showing who does what ; RACI is one kind of RAM. It is used for both planning (assigning work) and tracking (checking each task has an owner), and makes authority, accountability and responsibility visible. The “who” can be an individual, team or department , and rows or columns can have totals (e.g. the number of contributors on a task). Team Models

The two early philosophies: decentralized/democratic (the team decides together) and centralized/autocratic (one person decides). The variation in between, controlled decentralized , has a leader who coordinates while sub-groups decide within their own areas. Team Models • Two early philosophies • Decentralized/democratic • Centralized/autocratic • Variation • Controlled Decentralized 26
Team Models

The business team is the most common model in software and general business. A technical lead plus the team (the others at equal status), hierarchical with one principal contact. It can be a strong hierarchy (the lead has clear authority) or a loose one (the lead facilitates rather than commands). It is adaptable and general. The variation, the democratic team : all decisions are made by the whole team. Teams often start as a business team and evolve toward democratic as they mature, gain trust and develop shared norms. Team models, in slide order: B usy D evelopers C ode S uper S oftware. Business, Democratic, Chief-programmer, Skunk works, SWAT. What’s the difference between a Business Team and a Democratic Team? Team Models • Business Team: commonly used in software projects and general business environments. • Most common model • Technical lead + team (rest of team at equal status) • Hierarchical with one principal contact • Can be strong (The lead has clear authority and control) or loose hierarchy (The lead facilitates rather than commands—more collaborative) • Adaptable and general • Variation: Democratic Team • All decisions made by whole team • The Business Team is often the default starting point—especially in structured environments. But as teams mature, gain trust, and develop shared norms, they may evolve toward a Democratic Team model. 27
Democratic team organization

In a democratic team the group acts as a whole and comes to a consensus on decisions affecting the system. The leader is only the external interface and does not allocate specific work items. Work is discussed by the whole group and tasks are allocated by ability and experience . It succeeds only when all members are experienced and competent ; such teams are also called self-organizing teams (as in Scrum). Democratic team organization • The group acts as a whole and comes to a consensus on decisions affecting the system • The group leader serves as the external interface of the group but does not allocate specific work items • Rather, work is discussed by the group as a whole and tasks are allocated according to ability and experience • This approach is successful for groups where all members are experienced and competent • Sometimes known as self-organizing teams. 28
Agile programming groups

Agile groups are variants of democratic organization: some management decisions (estimating, task assignment) are delegated to the group members. In XP , programmers work in pairs and take collective responsibility for the code: anyone can change any part, and nobody “owns” a module. Agile programming groups • Agile programming groups are variants of democratic organization • In Agile programming groups, some ‘management’ decisions are delegated to group members • In XP, Programmers work in pairs and take a collective responsibility for code that is developed 29
Team Models

The chief-programmer (surgical) team , from IBM in the 1970s: a superstar writes the core code, supported by specialists, like a surgeon supported by anesthetists and nurses. The backup programmer (co-pilot) is equally skilled, shadows and reviews the chief, and can step in if needed. The program clerk manages documentation and version control; the administrator handles admin work; the tool-smith builds and maintains tools and environments; the language lawyer is the deep expert in the programming language. Issues: it is difficult to achieve (superstars are rare) and has ego problems on both sides. It can suit creative projects or tactical execution. In large teams communication paths grow with roughly the square of the team size. The exact formula is n(n − 1) / 2 : 50 people → 1,225 paths (the slide rounds to 1,200); 7 people → 21. So large teams must formalize communication, always use a hierarchy , and break into units of optimal size: always fewer than 10 (seven plus or minus one). The optimal team size is 4–6 developers plus a tech lead, with QA, operations and design on top. Small teams inspire stronger identification and cohesiveness . Motivating people

At work you can assume physiological and safety needs are satisfied (salary, safe workplace). So social, esteem and self-realization needs are the ones that matter for a manager. But if a lower need stays unmet for a long time (e.g. job security during layoffs), people shift focus downwards to it until it is satisfied again, and higher motivators stop working. Motivating people • People’s Motivations depend on satisfying needs • It can be assumed that physiological and safety needs are satisfied • Social, esteem and self-realization (self-actualization) needs are most significant from a managerial viewpoint • If a lower set of needs is continually unmet for an extended period of time, the individual will temporarily shift focus downwards those needs – dropping down to that level until those lower needs are reasonably satisfied again. 39

How to satisfy each need. Social : communal facilities (shared spaces, break rooms) and informal communication (team chats, lunch). Personality types

The needs hierarchy is an over-simplification ; motivation also depends on personality type . Task-oriented : the motivation is the work itself (they love solving the problem). Self-oriented : the work is a means to personal goals (get rich, buy a house, travel). Interaction-oriented : the main motivation is the presence and actions of co-workers; they come to work because they like being with the team. SIT : Self-oriented, Interaction-oriented, Task-oriented. A developer works mainly to save for a house. Motivation balance

Real people have elements of each class , and the balance changes with personal circumstances (a new baby makes someone more self-oriented for a while). People are also motivated by being part of a group and culture : they go to work partly for the people they work with. Group composition: group working

Most software engineering is a group activity ; non-trivial schedules can’t be met by one person. Group interaction is a key determinant of performance, so how the group works together matters as much as individual skill. Flexibility in group composition is limited : managers rarely pick an ideal team and must do their best with the people available. A group whose members all share the same motivation is a problem. Group cohesiveness

In a cohesive group members consider the group more important than any individual in it. Leadership

Leadership is the capacity to mobilize a group to solve its most challenging problems; it is wrong to think it is about authority. Technical leadership (a.k.a. authority) works when the problem can be solved by known means : the leader directs, instructs and applies best practices. Adaptive leadership is needed when the problem can’t be solved by known means (complex or novel). It requires learning by the leader as well as the group, and often means leading with good questions that provoke thinking. It also needs deep clarity of purpose to keep the team anchored, e.g. in brainstorming the leader stops the discussion drifting into unimportant arguments and brings it back to the essential questions. Leadership • Leadership is the capacity to mobilize a group to solve the most challenging problems (wrong to think that leadership is about authority) • Two types of leadership: • Technical leadership (a.k.a. authority) motivates people when the problem can be solved by known means: the leader directs, instructs and applies best practices. • Adaptive leadership motivates people to solve problems that cannot be solved by known means (needed when the problem is complex or novel) • Requires learning on the part of the leader as well as the group (facilitate learning and research) • Often involves leading with good questions (provoke thinking, guide inquiry) • Requires a deep clarity of purpose (to keep the team anchored toward its goals) : Example: during brainstorming meetings, the leader is the one that needs to stop the conversation from diverging to unimportant arguments, problems and bring the discussion back to the essential questions. 71

Working toward consensus

The steps: pose the problem or decision → solicit input on options → discuss and weigh pros and cons of each → work toward the options with the most benefit for the project . When the best option is clear, work with its opponents to help them buy in: persuade, don’t dictate . Consensus takes longer than a mandate but pays off in commitment. Beware passive-aggressive agreement : people who say yes but don’t act on it. It is just hidden (subsumed) conflict. The order matters here: P lease S it D own, W e C onfirm. Methodology Concepts

A process is a collection of work activities, actions and tasks performed when some work product is to be created. A process model (life cycle) is an abstract description of a process that shows one view of it: waterfall, iterative, spiral, evolutionary. A methodology is an instantiation of a process model: concrete and prescriptive, the conventions a group agrees to, “how we work around here”. So Scrum at your company is a methodology; “iterative” is the model behind it. Waterfall, iterative and spiral are examples of: Methodology Concepts • Process • A collection of work activities, actions and tasks that are performed when some work product is to be created • Process Model or Life Cycle • An abstract description of a software process that presents one view of that process • Waterfall, Iterative, Spiral, Evolutionary, etc. • Process Methodology or Methodology • Instantiations of process models – tend to be prescriptive. • The conventions that a group agrees to – “How we work around here” 5

Sequential (‘waterfall’) methodology

The term waterfall comes from Winston Royce’s 1970 paper on managing large software systems. Royce used the pure sequential waterfall as an example of an ill-conceived, risk-prone practice. Waterfall system development model

Waterfall is a highly sequential process: no phase overlaps. Failure symptoms: protracted integration and late design breakage (everything is integrated at the end, where design flaws appear) and late risk resolution (the big risks only show in testing). Many organizations still follow it, usually a modified version . Evolutionary methodologies

An evolutionary methodology is iterative and incremental: you can start with incomplete, imperfect knowledge . It is like a jigsaw puzzle : neither top-down nor bottom-up, but accretionary and convergent (pieces accumulate until the picture emerges). Advantages: an architecture that evolves logically, effective management of changing requirements and planning changes, continuous integration , early understanding (the “Hello world!” effect) and ongoing risk assessment . It is incremental at both the macro (project) and micro (team) levels. Evolutionary methodologies • An evolutionary methodology follows an iterative and incremental approach that allows the start of development with incomplete, imperfect knowledge • An iterative and incremental process is like solving a jigsaw puzzle: neither top-down nor bottom-up but accretionary and convergent • An iterative and incremental process offers these advantages: • Logical progress toward evolving a robust architecture • Effective management of changing requirements • Effective means to address changes in planning • Ability to perform continuous integration • Early understanding of the system (the ‘Hello world!’ effect) • Ongoing risk assessment • Evolutionary methodologies are incremental at both the macro (project- scale) and micro (working team) process levels 24

Product backlog item states

Ready for consideration : tentative, high-level ideas that may change radically or be dropped. Ready for refinement : agreed as important, with a reasonably clear definition, but needing work to understand and refine. Ready for implementation : detailed enough to estimate and build, with dependencies identified. CRIb , already in order: Consideration, Refinement, Implementation. Product backlog item states • Ready for consideration These are high-level ideas and feature descriptions that will be considered for inclusion in the product. They are tentative so may radically change or may not be included in the final product. • Ready for refinement The team has agreed that this is an important item that should be implemented as part of the current development. There is a reasonably clear definition of what is required. However, work is needed to understand and refine the item. • Ready for implementation The PBI has enough detail for the team to estimate the effort involved and to implement the item. DevOps vs. Project Management

With continuous CI/CD, DevOps can seem at odds with project management , which follows timelines with a start and end. DevOps vs. Project Management • Given the fluid nature of DevOps and its continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) process, the methodology may seem at odds with project management strategies that tend to follow timelines with a start and endpoint (waterfall style of PM). • These Project Management approaches (timelines, Gantt charts, milestones, deadlines, etc.) seem more closely aligned with traditional software delivery methods like the waterfall approach. • However, project management styles can adapt to fit the parameters of the DevOps pipeline (flexibility and rapid iteration): breaking work into sprints, focusing on iterative progress, and embracing change. • The key is to shift the focus away from the one final product and instead refactor the timeline to follow the agile approach of incremental deliveries at the end of each sprint. 80
What is DevOps project management?

DevOps project management is a union of the two: PM tailored to support the DevOps model. PMs act as coordinators between contributors and trackers of timelines and dependencies: making collaboration smooth, removing bottlenecks, resolving conflicts. They must also be closely aligned with the DevOps team and have a deep understanding of the development process . What is DevOps project management? • DevOps project management is a union between the two disciplines where project management is tailored to and supports the DevOps model. • In a DevOps project management approach, project managers serve as coordinators between multiple contributors and as trackers of timelines and dependencies (ensure team members collaborate smoothly, removing bottlenecks and resolving conflicts) • However, project managers also need to be closely aligned with the DevOps team and bring a deep understanding of the development process and skills needed to create the end product. • There are several best practices that project managers should follow to achieve this integration with the DevOps pipeline. 81

Fixed-price: contractor carries the risk (and prices it in). Cost-reimbursable: buyer carries most of the risk. Fixed price → risk on the SELLER. Cost reimbursable → risk on the BUYER. Strategies for negative risks or threats

Mitigate = reduce probability and/or impact (more tests, simpler processes, reliable vendors). Accept: passive = just document; active = set aside a reserve. Running extra performance tests to lower the chance of a slow release is: Active acceptance means setting aside reserves of funds, time or resources. Strategies for negative risks or threats • Mitigation • Risk mitigation attempts to reduce the probability of a risk event and/or its impacts to an acceptable level • Risk mitigation takes the viewpoint that fixing a problem earlier in a project is less costly than fixing it later • Examples: Performing more tests, using simpler processes, perform simulations, choose vendors for reliability over cost • Risk acceptance • The risk is acknowledged, but no action is taken unless the risk occurs • Appropriate when it is not possible or cost-effective to address a speciﬁc risk in any other way • Passive acceptance simply documents that the acceptance strategy has been adopted and leaves the project team to deal with the risks • Active acceptance set aside risk reserves, such as a pool of funds, time, or resources to be used in response to a risk event 69
Strategies for negative risks or threats

Contingency plans do NOT reduce P or I. They define what to do when it happens. Example: disaster recovery plan. Strategies for negative risks or threats • Risk contingency plans q • Contingency planning involves planning alternatives to deal with the risks, should they occur • Contingency plans do not seek to reduce the probability or impact of risks, the strategy accepts that the risk may occur and plans ways to respond to the risk • A contingency plan is executed when the risk event occurs • Contingency plans must be in place well before the time the risk may occur • Contingency plans are developed for risks: • With very high impact or: • With response strategies that may themselves be risky (require preparation) • Contingency plans usually entail a signiﬁcant alternative path through part of the project • Example: disaster recovery plan 70

Contingency allowance = reserve pool. Fallback = Plan B if the primary response fails. Opportunities: exploit (make sure it happens), share (give to a third party who can capture it). Sidebar: Residual and secondary risks

Secondary = new risks CAUSED by your response. Residual = risk LEFT OVER after responding → contingency reserve. After hiring an expert consultant as a risk response, the consultant falls ill. This is a: Sidebar: Residual and secondary risks • Secondary risks arise as a result of implementing a risk response, they are the risks inherent in the response • Identify and plan responses for secondary risks using tools such as fallback plans • Example: O-O/RDB expert consultant becomes ill • Residual risks are those that cannot be effectively dealt with within the rest of the risk plan • Example: Some risk may remain. Residual risks are usually dealt with through contingency reserves • Example: Developer skills risks (resource planning risk) associated with alternate database solution 73

Estimation

Why hard: evolving requirements, technical unknowns, team skill/availability, external dependencies. Basic process: size → effort (person-months) → schedule. S.E.S.: Size, Effort, Schedule, always in that order. What is the correct order of the basic estimation process? Estimation • Why it’s difficult: evolving requirements; technical unknowns; team skill and availability; external dependencies. • Created, used or refined during • Strategic planning: Aligns project goals with organizational capacity and timelines • Feasibility study and/or SOW(Statement of Work: document that defines the scope, deliverables, timelines and responsibilities): Determines whether the project is viable and worth pursuing • Proposals: Helps justify cost, scope, and timeline to stakeholders or clients • Vendor and sub-contractor evaluation: Compares bids, assesses realism, and negotiates contracts • Project planning (iteratively): Refines estimates as more information becomes available • Basic process 1) Estimate the size of the product 2) Estimate the effort (person-months) 3) Estimate the schedule • NOTE: Not all of these steps are always explicitly performed 4
Estimation

No exact estimate exists. Software estimates are commonly off by 25–100%. Estimation • Remember, an “exact estimate” is not possible • Estimate how long will it take you to get home from class today • On what basis did you do that? • Experience is useful • Likely as an “average” (based on historical data), probable estimation • For most software projects there is no such ‘average’ Most software estimations are off by 25-100% 5
Estimation: definitions

Target date = from business/marketing. Committed date = what the team agrees after planning. Don’t commit to targets early. Bigger project → more variance (7% small … 51% very large). A target date is one the team commits to after building a schedule. Estimation: definitions • Target vs. Committed Dates • Target: Proposed by business or marketing • Do not commit to this too soon! (Learn to say no and how to say it) • Committed: Team agrees to this (based on actual planning) • After you’ve developed a schedule • As project size increases, so does uncertainty: • Small projects (10-99 FPs), variance of 7% from post-requirements estimates • Medium (100-999 FPs), 22% variance • Large (1000-9999 FPs) 38% variance • Very large (> 10K FPs) 51% variance -> push back on target dates, understand that variance is normal 6
Cone of Uncertainty

Early estimates can be 0.25× to 4× the real value; the cone narrows as you learn. Ch 1.2, slide 40 : Estimates change as the project evolves At the feasibility stage, the cone of uncertainty says estimates may range from: Cone of Uncertainty • The upper curve represents the maximum possible overestimation. • The lower curve represents the maximum possible underestimation. • Over time, these curves converge toward 1x, meaning your estimate becomes more accurate and reliable. • Early estimates (e.g., during feasibility or proposal stages) can be wildly inaccurate — anywhere from 0.25x to 4x the actual scope. • As the project moves through requirements gathering, design, and development, uncertainty decreases 7
